old: Sit down. You've got that look people get when they've been carrying something heavy up a hill.
new: I called it my inn this morning. Out loud, to Oda. I did not correct myself.
why: Identical to her before-line; after her arc closes she stops calling the inn Josie's place, and that is the fact the line should carry.

old: I put a loaf by for you. Don't tell Pip, he counts them.
new: I put a loaf by for you. Same as you put one by for me in February, only mine is better.
why: Identical to her before-line; echoes the same object and lands her Act IV beat, being fed by you, without naming the feeling.

old: The Hearth's been lit in this room for thirty years. Some of those years it was the only thing that was.
new: The Hearth is lit, the oven is lit and the rooms upstairs are lit. Three fires. I keep counting them.
why: Identical to her before-line; same cadence and the same hearth, but the count has changed from one fire to three.

old: Eat something. I'm not asking.
new: Eat something. I cooked for fifteen tonight and there is still too much, which is the right amount.
why: Identical to her before-line; keeps the imperative and swaps in the population count the bossbar is showing.

old: Fish aren't biting. Sit down anyway.
new: Fish aren't biting. Doesn't matter — the tomatoes are.
why: Identical to her before-line; same shrug, new fact, and it points at the greenhouse her arc ends in.

old: Quiet down here. That's not a complaint.
new: Boat's mended. Took one afternoon. I had been calling it a week's work since before you came.
why: Identical to her before-line; answers the beached boat her before-pool keeps refusing to talk about.

old: Good spot's past the reeds. Don't tell everyone.
new: Good spot's past the reeds. Tell people. I have decided I don't mind a crowd.
why: Identical to her before-line; inverts the secret into an invitation, which is the whole point of the docks being rebuilt.

old: Kettle's on. Everything else can wait ten minutes; it always could.
new: Kettle's on. The book is open on the table and there are two chairs at it now.
why: Identical to his before-line; keeps the kettle and the ten-minute patience, changes the fact that he is no longer working alone.

old: The hedge doesn't need me. That's rather why I like it.
new: Josie asked me to stay. Four years I told people it was the hedge.
why: Identical to his before-line; his arc is admitting exactly this, and the hedge stays in the sentence as the cover story.

old: Josie planted the first row of that. I only ever kept it trimmed.
new: Josie planted the first row. I have planted the second, which took me rather longer than it should have.
why: Identical to his before-line; same row of hedge, same dry self-deprecation, and he has finally added to it instead of trimming it.

old: Green tea, or the strong one? The strong one is a decision.
new: Green tea, or the strong one? Nobody has been ill since November, so have the strong one.
why: Identical to his before-line; keeps the joke and quietly reports the cold snap nobody got sick in.

old: Look at this rock. No — properly look at it. Sorry. Sorry.
new: This one has quartz all through it. Nobody in this valley cares about quartz. I care enormously.
why: Repeats element 0's 'Look at this rock. No, really look' joke, so two of Tobin's four before-lines are the same beat; new line keeps the obsession and adds a mineral and a confession.

old: Look at this rock. No — properly look at it. Sorry. Sorry.
new: Look at this rock. It is the same rock. I keep it in my pocket now, which Bram says is normal.
why: Identical to his before-line; same rock, same apology-shaped energy, and Bram's approval is the changed fact.

old: I've marked it twice. The second set's in pink. Ignore the pink.
new: The pink marks were right. Nobody has said so out loud, and I am being very calm about it.
why: Identical to his before-line; the pink marks he told you to ignore turned out to be the seam.

old: I haven't slept, but that's not new information.
new: I haven't slept. The rig comes up the road when the road dries, and the road is drying.
why: Identical to his before-line; keeps the joke's shape and hangs it on the quarry rig he is now responsible for.

old: Eat the purple one first. Always the purple one first.
new: I found a red one. I did not eat it. I am learning to not eat first.
why: Repeats element 0's 'Eat the purple one first' verbatim; new line keeps Wisp's slightly-wrong grammar and changes the fact (he is learning restraint).

old: You walk far today? Sit. I keep the good toadstools.
new: You walk far today? Sit. I keep the good toadstools in the inn now, in a cupboard with a door.
why: Identical to his before-line; same welcome, and the marsh has become a town with jobs and signs in it.

old: Marsh is quiet, town is loud. Both is good. Different good.
new: Marsh is quiet, town is loud. I sleep in the loud one now. Is strange. I like.
why: Identical to his before-line; the two-places-one-place choice is made instead of admired.

old: My people ask about you. I say: is the one who came and asked.
new: My people do not ask about you now. They ask you. Is better, I think.
why: Identical to his before-line; the villages are one place, so the go-between is out of a job.

old: Eat the purple one first. Always the purple one first.
new: Purple one grows in the warm glass house in winter now. I did not know it could do that.
why: Identical to his before-line; the purple mushroom is kept and the greenhouse is the changed fact.

old: I named the duck after you. Do not be weird about it.
new: The duck is called Biscuit. I decided it in about one second and I am not changing it.
why: Contradicts canon: Q11 summons a duck named Biscuit and the quest text says Pip names it Biscuit; this line still says he named it after the player, which the design doc records as the one line that could never render.

old: The duck went in the water bucket. On purpose, I think. It's fine.
new: Biscuit went in the water trough in front of everybody at supper. She meant to. I saw her decide.
why: Identical to his before-line; same duck, same joke, and it uses her canon name and a full room.

old: I'm allowed in the mill now if I don't touch anything. I touch nothing.
new: I'm allowed to touch things in the mill now. Bram showed me which ones. I remember all of them.
why: Identical to his before-line; exactly inverts the fact, which is what a closed arc is supposed to do.

old: Aunt Marnie says I ask too many questions. How many is too many?
new: Aunt Marnie says I still ask too many questions. I asked her how many. She is thinking about it.
why: Identical to his before-line; keeps the question and gives it an answer that is still pending.

old: My satchel has a real buckle. Not a pretend one. A real one.
new: I'm the one who rings the bell. Nobody else rings it. That was the deal and everybody heard it.
why: Identical to his before-line; lands the bell Josie asked for in Entry 5 and Pip casts at Q89 — the promise map's last row.

old: Warm inn. Warm soup. We stay now, I think. Yes. We stay.
new: Floor is warm and soup is hot. We stay now, I think. Yes. We stay.
why: Opens with 'Warm inn. Warm soup.' word for word from Wisp's Q58 scene line, so two frog-folk say the same sentence; the repetition and the meaning are kept, the phrasing is not.

old: There you are. Mind the gate.
new: Mind the gate. Those two would walk to the lake if you let them.
why: 'There you are. Mind the gate.' opens with the same three words as her headline greeting and 'the gate' is the only thing in it; new line keeps the instruction and adds a picture and a hen with an opinion.

old: No hen close enough. Stand in the pen.
new: She won't lay from over there. Stand in the pen with her.
why: Error-state line written as a notice, not a person — 'No hen close enough' has no verb and nothing withheld; same instruction, in Marnie's mouth.

old: Not there. Fifteen houses, a square and a mill go in around that stake, and I will not have them in your dooryard. Walk on up the road until the chimney is small behind you, then drive it.
new: Not there — a square and a mill go in around that stake. Walk up until the chimney is small behind you, then drive it.
why: 188 chars against the 120-char chat cap, and 'fifteen houses' contradicts the counter: fifteen is the population, not the building count. Instruction and landmark preserved.

locator: line 675 v.say(player,'Josie',...) (Q7 stake too close, flat pad)
old: Flat enough, that. Too near, though — fifteen houses and a square would end up in your garden. Keep walking; you will know it when the chimney is small behind you.
new: Flat enough, that. Too near, though — the square would end up in your garden. Keep walking until the chimney is small.
why: 163 chars against the 120-char cap, and repeats the same 'fifteen houses' miscount as the other too-close line. Same beat, same landmark, inside cap.

locator: line 688 v.say(player,'Josie',...) (Q7 stake, nudge after searching)
old: Nothing flat up here? Then flatten a five-by-five and stake that. Level is the whole requirement.
new: Nothing flat up here? Then flatten a five-by-five yourself and stake that. Level is all it has to be.
why: 'Level is the whole requirement' is spec-sheet register in a dead woman's mouth; the instruction is unchanged and the last clause is now speech.

old: Three empty houses, three beds, three blankets. People arrive in spring, and beds should be made before they get here.
new: Three empty houses, three beds, three blankets. I want them turned down before anybody gets to the top of the road.
why: Second sentence explains the rule instead of showing it ('beds should be made before they get here'); new close is an image and it still foreshadows Tess, Mab and Corin.

old: Year two on the board, and it is a longer list than last spring. I have written the bottom four lines out exactly as they were.
new: Year two on the board. Longer list than last spring, and the bottom four lines are still in Josie's hand.
why: 127 chars against the 120-char cap and 'exactly as they were' withholds something the player cannot name; naming the handwriting makes it a picture and a hook.

old: {Name}'s story is closed. That's {n} of eight in my book.
new: {Name}'s account is closed. That's {n} of eight in my book.
why: 'Story is closed' is author-voice about the player's progress; 'account' is Oda's own noun and keeps both placeholders and the identical sentence shape.

old: Josie: "Four walls and a door. That is a house. What you do next makes it a home."
new: Josie: "Four walls and a door. The mat is where my bed was; that corner stays warm until about four in the morning."
why: 'That is a house. What you do next makes it a home' is the banned it's-not-X-it's-Y summary and would fit any game; replaced with a fact about the marked mat, so it confirms Q3's instruction instead of competing with it.

old: Josie: "Bram surveyed that flat twice and never drove the stake. You drove it. That is the whole difference."
new: Josie: "Stake's in. Bram will tell you he chose the spot. Let him."
why: Repeats the Bram-surveyed-it-twice fact the green-light line said seconds earlier, then summarises the theme ('that is the whole difference'); new line is the same beat with a joke and no restatement.
